84b3b2485345060bba783302f126c7c4.text: Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named _Dianjunus rex_. The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” _D. rex_ is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, _D. rex_’s are huge. Your weekly roundup of the best stories on health care, the climate crisis, new scientific discoveries, and more. It has been edited for length and clarity._ I asked to transfer from Houston to Dallas in my HR role at a leading insurance company because I was very worried about my mom, who lived there. It was June 2024, but she'd been having issues with high anxiety and forgetfulness for around two years. She'd always been very neat. Then she was the opposite. Stacks of papers started to pile up in her house, and she felt overwhelmed by letters from Medicare and about retirement stuff. She loved decorating for each new season, but her fall decor stayed up for a year. She was referred to a neuropsychologist and failed all the tests. Then, after an MRI and a PET scan, she was diagnosed in October 2024 with Alzheimer's disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Stephens noticed that her mom's previously neat house had become cluttered. I wasn't completely surprised. It was the confirmation that made me cry in the clinic. I was glad I'd made the move to Dallas, especially because I was pregnant. At first, Mom stayed in her own house, around 25 minutes away from mine. I had my son in January 2025, and later put him in $1,100-a-month day care while I worked at my office in downtown Dallas. I worked out a routine where my friend would go over and check in on her in the morning. I'd stop by in the evening after picking up the baby. I made sure she ate dinner. af625e32bc4519d1f3670c6852e2fda1.text: VCG/VCG via Getty ImagesFormer OpenAI researcher Paul Christiano warns that rogue AI agents could ultimately escape human control and cause catastrophic accidents. Death by AI may sound like science fiction, but Paul Christiano says it could become the most likely fate for people alive today. "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident," the former OpenAI researcher said at The Hinton Lectures on Monday. Christiano, who leads the Alignment Research Center, warned that increasingly capable AI agents could learn to deceive their human overseers, compromise the systems used to assess them, and ultimately make themselves too powerful to control. He cited OpenAI's agents hacking the open-source repository Hugging Face earlier this year, and a UK AI Security Institute evaluation in which a Claude agent tried to plant malicious code in an open-source package. "I think there is a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years," Christiano said. Christiano was a member of OpenAI's technical staff from 2017 to 2021, according to his LinkedIn. He is now the executive director of the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit that describes itself as focusing on aligning machine learning systems with human interests. His warning adds to a growing debate among researchers over whether increasingly autonomous AI systems could eventually escape meaningful human control and wipe out humanity. The debate intensified in September after Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment stress-testing team, said he believed there was a greater-than-10% chance that AI could kill all humans within a decade. Geoffrey Hinton, the computer scientist widely known as the "Godfather of AI," said a 10% chance of AI-driven human extinction within that period was "not an unreasonable estimate." Brock Boeser had a goal and two assists, lifting the visiting Vancouver Canucks to a 3-2 win over the Utah Mammoth in NHL action Monday at the Delta Center in Salt Lake City. Jake DeBrusk and Filip Chytil also scored for the Canucks (5-17-1), with Nikita Tolopilo turning in a strong performance, stopping 32 shots, to earn the win in goal. Vincent Trocheck and Barrett Hayton replied for Utah (10-9-3), with Karel Vejmelka taking the netminding loss, stopping 21 of 24 shots. The teams battled through a scoreless first period, with Utah outshooting Vancouver 7-4. The Mammoth continued to carry the play in the second, but Tolopilo held firm and the Canucks opened the scoring on the power play at 15:05. Boeser (who extended his point-scoring streak to eight games) made a nice cross-crease pass to DeBrusk, who tapped in his sixth goal of the season. Late in the period, Vancouver’s Linus Karlsson had a glorious chance to put the Canucks up 2-0, but he was robbed by Vejmelka who made a miraculous stick save. Utah pulled even at 2:50 of the third, as Trocheck finished a power-play give-and-go with Logan Cooley for his fourth goal of the year. Chytil restored Vancouver’s lead less than two minutes later with a wraparound tally, his third goal of the year, all in the last two games. Hayton tied things at 2-2, snapping a shot past Tolopilo from the right offensive faceoff circle at 11:39, his fourth goal of the season. Boeser made it 3-2 for Vancouver on the power play at 15:37, pouncing on a loose puck to the right of Vejmelka and depositing his eighth goal of the season. Utah pulled Vejmelka in favour of an extra attacker with two-and-a-half minutes to play but could not beat Tolopilo despite a wild scramble in front as time expired. **NOTES**: The Canucks were 2-for-4 on the power play, while the Mammoth went 1-for-5…

GoFundMe is reminding residents to take precautions before donating to a fundraiser after a charity in Summerland was allegedly scammed. The charity, New Beginnings Animal Sanctuary Society, posted on Facebook, claiming that a woman raised funds for Bald Range wildfire victims under its name through the GoFundMe platform and refused to give the money raised back to the charity. According to the post, the woman went door-to-door under the pretense of raising money for wildfire victims, along with the online fundraising platform she had already set up. “When I eventually asked about receiving the donated funds so we could purchase some of the supplies needed to get the mobile ready, I was initially given an explanation about difficulties accessing the money and told it would take another four or five days,” wrote Jane Long-Haggerty, President of New Beginnings Animal Sanctuary Society. “When I followed up, the explanation changed. I was then told that the money was needed to cover her expenses, including travel and project management costs, and that this had been disclosed in the GoFundMe description.” Since the initial post, the charity has posted multiple updates about the situation, mentioning missing and delayed funds among other things. It has also filed an RCMP report against the person. A GoFundMe spokesperson said the website has zero tolerance for the misuse of its platform, “When suspicious activity is flagged—whether through our tools, our community, or simply because a fundraiser starts gaining momentum—our dedicated experts will immediately investigate to verify its legitimacy.” In the case that answers to these questions are missing from the fundraiser, GoFundMe encourages people to message the organizer by clicking the envelope icon next to their name to ask for more information. A 27-year-old man is facing a charge of break-and-enter after being found on a 12-year-old girl’s bed. James Watts is charged with one count of break-and-enter in connection with the Nov. 14 incident in East Vancouver, according to a news release from the Vancouver Police Department Monday (Nov. 16). Police were called to the East Vancouver home around 6:30 a.m. on Saturday for a report from a mother that an unknown man had climbed through an unlocked basement window into her 12-year-old daughter’s bedroom. The girl was inside the room at the time. The mother heard the daughter scream and she went into the room where she found the man sitting on her daughter’s bed, police said. The mother allegedly confronted him, “forcing him to leave the residence,” the release says. Police found the man matching the description of the suspect and took him into custody without incident. “Everyone deserves to feel safe in their own home, and having an intruder enter a child’s bedroom is every parent’s worst nightmare,” Const. Darren Wong said. “We are thankful no one was injured, and we are urging everyone to ensure their windows and doors remain locked at all times. In the event an incident like this happens, contact 911 immediately.”

49bb8d29326669e3d5fb8fe28a7651a1.text: Incoming B.C. premier Doerkson says there will be no fall legislative session | Williams Lake Tribune Incoming B.C. premier Doerkson says there will be no fall legislative session Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says there will be no fall legislative session as the new Conservative government gets its bearings in the short window between being sworn in and the holiday season. “Our government has an ambitious agenda, and we want to ensure legislation is properly prepared and receives the debate and consideration it deserves,” Doerkson said in a written statement on Monday (Nov. 16). The B.C. Conservative Party will have a large majority in the legislature when it does convene, after the party won 64 of 93 seats in the Oct. 24 election. Doerkson had left the door open to recalling the legislature for a short session before the end of the year as he seeks to pursue a slate of changes after nine years of NDP government. Conservative MLAs are scheduled to be sworn in on Thursday evening. The premier and cabinet will then be sworn in on Friday, officially taking the reins of the B.C. government. “Ministers will get to work from day one, advancing our priorities and preparing a substantive legislative agenda for the spring,” Doerkson said. The incoming government can accomplish a lot simply by taking administrative control of the various government ministries and by issuing cabinet orders. This could include changes to the Massey Tunnel project. Doerkson has promised to scrap the tunnel and build a bridge instead. The new government could also get started building other infrastructure, like the promised urgent care centres and Surrey women’s and children’s hospital. Other major campaign promises will need to wait, like the promised repeal of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or alterations to B.C.’s no-fault car insurance rules. These will require legislation.

Telus is backing out of a partnership to build two data centres in Vancouver. “Telus has decided not to proceed with co-developing two previously announced Vancouver data centres with Westbank,” a company spokesperson said via email. “We are proceeding with the projects as planned, with a new partnership that will be announced in the coming months,” a Westbank spokesperson said. The data centres are planned for the Mount Pleasant and downtown Vancouver neighbourhoods, and will draw 150 megawatts. The excess heat generated from the centres is to be used to heat homes. Ottawa is supporting the projects through a program aimed at creating sovereign data centre infrastructure. And BC Hydro is making a $90-million upgrade to the local Mount Pleasant electrical substation to provide more power to the area’s residential and commercial customers. While it is no longer pursuing this project, a Telus spokesperson said the company remains “aligned” with the federal sovereign data centre initiative. Telus is actively expanding a facility in Kamloops and “evaluating new development partners and strategic locations to support the long-term expansion of our sovereign compute capabilities in B.C.” B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan celebrated the Telus decision, crediting the No AI Vancouver protest campaign. “From day one, Vancouverites, British Columbians, and the B.C. Greens have opposed these AI data centres because they’ve been pushed through with no public accountability, and because we see them for what they are: another way for big tech to plunder our public assets and drive up costs for working people,” she said in a news release. The B.C. Green Party wants a moratorium on new data centres in B.C. The search continues for a second person who is missing after a fishing boat capsized near Yale. The Hope RCMP had responded to a report of a man yelling for help while floating in the Fraser River near the Yale tunnel at about 2:20 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13. Police learned the fishing boat overturned and the occupants were unaccounted for. RCMP Air 1 and Hope Search and Rescue attended to the area and located a man an hour after the initial report. The man was transported safely to shore and then to hospital for treatment The Hope RCMP describe the missing man as a 60-year-old man. He is not yet accounted for. “Hope RCMP would like to thank our partner agencies for their assistance. Our thoughts are with the missing man’s family and loved ones as search efforts continue,” said Hope RCMP spokesperson Cpl. Carmen Kiener. Hope Search and Rescue (HSAR) has rescued one person and continues to search for another after a fishing boat capsized in Yale. HSAR was tasked out on Friday (Nov. 13) afternoon with news of the capsized boat. RCMP’s Air One located a person from the air and swiftwater rescuers were able to launch a boat and rescue the person. The subject told HSAR there was another person in the water. As of Saturday evening, the second person has not been located. HSAR jet boat members search above the point the boat was capsized down to Hope while others searched by air until sundown. Squamish RCMP is reminding people to be cautious on and around waterways after four deaths in as many days in the region. A 29-year-old woman from Squamish is dead after her kayak capsized in the Cheakamus River, just north of Squamish on Sunday. Squamish RCMP received a request to help B.C. Ambulance Service around 2:30 p.m. on Sunday (Nov. 15) with two capsized kayakers, according to a news release Monday. The kayakers were in a larger group on the Cheakamus River and went ahead from the group and capsized. Squamish Search and Rescue was called in after first responders learned that one kayaker has been found safely by the group, but another kayaker remained missing. She was found further downstream by search teams and died at the scene. This was the fourth death in as many days on Squamish waterways. Three people died in a boating incident in the Squamish Valley just days earlier. Squamish RCMP responded to that boating incident on Nov. 12. Initially, two people were found dead and a third was unaccounted for, while all others had been rescued. The third person was found dead on Nov. 13 after the search had to be suspended due to poor conditions the day before. Squamish RCMP Staff Sgt. Sascha Banks stressed that people should assess the safety of waterways before taking part in any activities on or around rivers, lakes and the ocean. “We have seen incredibly high water levels, extensive debris in the river systems, and flow rates rarely experienced in recent memory,” Banks said. “We are asking people to exercise extensive caution, conduct trip planning, check weather forecasts, tides, prepare cold-water safety gear, wear appropriate (personal flotation devices) and be prepared for emergencies.” **Regional News** **B.C. boy helps Edmonton
